en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on Intimacy.
4. The Question on the Arising of the Path “Venerable Nāgasena, this has been said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the path that had not arisen.’”
And again it was said:
“I saw, monks, the ancient path, the ancient way, followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of old.
If, venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata is the arouser of the unarisen path, then how is it that he said, “I saw”?
"O monks, as for the statement: 'I am following the ancient path, the ancient straight way, trodden by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of old,' that is false.
If it was spoken by the Tathāgata—"
‘Bhikkhus, I have seen the ancient path, the ancient way, followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of old,’ then that statement—
‘Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the unarisen path’— is also false.
“This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the path not yet arisen.’”
And it was said:
“I have indeed seen, O bhikkhus, an ancient path, an ancient way, followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of old.
Both of these statements, Great King, are simply words of fact, because of the disappearance of the previous Tathāgatas.
In the absence of an instructor, the path disappeared; the Tathāgata, seeing with the eye of wisdom that path— which was crumbled, broken down,
hidden, closed off, and concealed, and no longer accessible— beheld it as traversed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past,
and for that reason he said:
“I have seen, monks, an ancient path, an ancient road, followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past,” he said.

Great King, because the path of the previous Tathāgatas had fallen into ruin, crumbled, become hidden, closed off, concealed, and impassable due to their disappearance and the absence of an instructor, the Tathāgata has now made it passable again; for that reason he said:
“Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the unarisen path.”
"In this case, Great King, when a wheel-turning monarch passes away, the jewel-treasure disappears into the midst of the mountain peaks;
it reappears through the right conduct of another wheel-turning monarch. Now, Great King, is that jewel-treasure his own creation?
"Certainly not, venerable sir; that jewel-treasure is simply natural, though it was brought forth by him."
“In the same way, great king, the Blessed One, perceiving with the eye of wisdom, brought forth and made passable that eightfold auspicious path which was natural,
practiced by previous Tathāgatas, yet— in the absence of an instructor— had fallen into ruin, crumbled away, become hidden,
closed off, concealed, and impassable; for that reason he said:”
“Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the path that has not yet arisen.

Or alternatively, Great King, just as a mother is called “the progenitor” because she gives birth to an existing child from her womb, even so, Great King, the Tathāgata—perceiving with the eye of wisdom the existing path that was broken, dilapidated, hidden, obstructed, concealed, and impassable—aroused it, made it passable; for that reason he said:
“Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the path not yet arisen.

Or again, Great King, just as when some man finds something that was lost, people say, “That person produced that article,” even so, Great King, the Tathāgata—seeing with the eye of wisdom the very path that existed, though it was broken, shattered, hidden, closed, concealed, and impassable—aroused it, made it passable; for that reason he said: [‘the Tathāgata...’]”
“Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the path that has not yet arisen.

Or again, Great King, just as when a certain man clears away a forest and brings forth the earth, people speak of it as “his earth,” even though this earth was not produced by him; yet, by virtue of that earth being his work, he is called the owner of the earth.

“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata, perceiving with wisdom that the path was indeed existing—though broken, decayed, hidden, shut off, concealed, and impassable—brought it forth and made it passable; for that reason he said:
‘Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the bringer forth of the path that had not been brought forth.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.”
The fourth question: On the arising of the path.
